claim: Ascidians are the closest living relatives of vertebrates.
source: Ascidians are the closest living relatives of vertebrates, and their study is important for understanding the evolutionary processes of oocyte maturation and ovulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies (Delsuc et al., 2006; Denoeud et al., 2010; Satoh et al., 2014; Horie et al., 2018) in the Introduction section.

claim: CiVP ultimately activated a maturation-promoting factor, leading to oocyte maturation via germinal vesicle breakdown.
source: CiVP ultimately activated a maturation-promoting factor, leading to oocyte maturation via germinal vesicle breakdown.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4B and 4C showing that MPF inhibition blocks CiVP-induced GVBD.

claim: CiErk1/2 induced expression of matrix metalloproteinase (CiMMP2/9/13) in the oocyte.
source: CiErk1/2 also induced expression of matrix metalloproteinase (CiMMP2/9/13) in the oocyte, resulting in collagen degradation in the outer follicular cell layer and liberation of fertile oocytes from the ovary.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data in Figure 5A and 5B showing CiMMP2/9/13 expression changes with MEK inhibition and CiVP stimulation.

claim: CiMMP2/9/13 resulted in collagen degradation in the outer follicular cell layer.
source: CiErk1/2 also induced expression of matrix metalloproteinase (CiMMP2/9/13) in the oocyte, resulting in collagen degradation in the outer follicular cell layer and liberation of fertile oocytes from the ovary.
evidence: This is supported by in situ zymography data in Figure 6 showing collagenase activity in the outer follicular cell layer.

claim: Incubating Ciona ovaries in ASW for 16 hr resulted in the liberation of numerous follicles.
source: Notably, incubating Ciona ovaries in ASW for 16 hr resulted in the liberation of numerous follicles (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed and documented in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Follicle liberation followed the rupture of the outer follicular cell layer.
source: Intriguingly, time-lapse imaging revealed that follicle liberation followed the rupture of the outer follicular cell layer (Figure 1B and Video 1), and we therefore defined this phenomenon as Ciona ovulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: Rupture of outer follicular cells was observed in an isolated follicle following GVBD.
source: Moreover, such rupture of outer follicular cells was also observed in an isolated follicle following GVBD (Figure 1C and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Video 2.

claim: Both oocyte maturation and ovulation can be studied in vitro using isolated immature/pre-ovulatory follicles.
source: These results demonstrated that both oocyte maturation and ovulation can be studied in vitro using isolated immature/pre-ovulatory follicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful observation of GVBD and ovulation in isolated follicles as shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Ciona follicles undergo major developmental stages: stage I (pre-vitellogenic), stage II (vitellogenic), stage III (post-vitellogenic and pre-GVBD), and stage IV (post-GVBD, that is, mature) oocytes.
source: In the Ciona ovary, follicles undergo the following major developmental stages: stage I (pre-vitellogenic), stage II (vitellogenic), stage III (post-vitellogenic and pre-GVBD), and stage IV (post-GVBD, that is, mature) oocytes (Prodon et al., 2006; Tosti et al., 2011; Silvestre et al., 2009).
evidence: This classification is based on previous studies cited (Prodon et al., 2006; Tosti et al., 2011; Silvestre et al., 2009).

claim: Ciona follicles were successfully fractionated using stainless steel sieves of varying particle sizes.
source: We fractionated Ciona follicles using stainless steel sieves of varying particle sizes. Each fraction collected (20, 38, 63, 90, or 150 μm) contained a major developmental stage of Ciona follicles (Prodon et al., 2006), namely (i) early stage I, (ii) late stage I to early stage II, (iii) early stage II to late stage II, (iv) late stage II to late stage III, or (v) stage IV oocytes, confirming that the all developmental stages were successfully fractionated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fractionation results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RNA-seq analysis of fractionated follicles indicated no stage to stage changes in the expression of most genes.
source: RNA-seq analysis of two sets of the fractionated follicles indicated no stage to stage changes in the expression of most genes; however, some differential expression of genes was detected between two consecutive stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1), suggesting the usefulness of this approach for identifying genes responsible for oocyte maturation and ovulation.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Some differential expression of genes was detected between two consecutive stages of follicle development.
source: RNA-seq analysis of two sets of the fractionated follicles indicated no stage to stage changes in the expression of most genes; however, some differential expression of genes was detected between two consecutive stages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1), suggesting the usefulness of this approach for identifying genes responsible for oocyte maturation and ovulation.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Late stage II follicles exhibited 12.5 ± 4.6% GVBD and 28.6 ± 4.3% ovulation.
source: Small follicles (192.1 ± 9.3 μm) exhibited 12.5 ± 4.6% GVBD and 28.6 ± 4.3% ovulation.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Early stage III follicles exhibited 63.9 ± 8.6% GVBD and 61.4 ± 10.8% ovulation.
source: In contrast, mid-size (214.3 ± 7.6 μm) and large (228.8 ± 7.0 μm) follicles exhibited 63.9 ± 8.6% and 91.8 ± 3.4% GVBD, respectively, and 61.4 ± 10.8% and 87.2 ± 1.5% ovulation, respectively, leading to their further respective categorization as 'early stage III' and 'late stage III' (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Late stage III follicles exhibited 91.8 ± 3.4% GVBD and 87.2 ± 1.5% ovulation.
source: In contrast, mid-size (214.3 ± 7.6 μm) and large (228.8 ± 7.0 μm) follicles exhibited 63.9 ± 8.6% and 91.8 ± 3.4% GVBD, respectively, and 61.4 ± 10.8% and 87.2 ± 1.5% ovulation, respectively, leading to their further respective categorization as 'early stage III' and 'late stage III' (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expression of only the CiVpr gene was specifically elevated, with peak expression at late stage II to late stage III.
source: Among the several receptors for known Ciona neuropeptides in the ovary (Kawada et al., 2008; Satake et al., 2004; Sekiguchi et al., 2012; Tello et al., 2005; Shiraishi et al., 2019), RNA-seq analysis of fractionated follicles indicated that the expression of only the CiVpr gene (KH.C9.885), a receptor for CiVP, was specifically elevated, with peak expression at late stage II to late stage III, a period that is thought to be crucial in the regulation of oocyte maturation and ovulation.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and confirmed by qRT-PCR.

claim: CiVpr mRNA was localized to the oocytes of late stage II follicles.
source: Ciona follicles are comprised of three types of cells: oocytes, test cells, and follicular cells, and in situ hybridization showed that CiVpr mRNA was localized to the oocytes of late stage II follicles (Figure 3A), in agreement with the results of RNA-seq and qRT-PCR analyses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CiVP acts on oocytes of late stage II follicles.
source: These results indicated that CiVP acts on oocytes of late stage II follicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of CiVpr mRNA to oocytes shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Treating late stage II follicles with CiVP for 24 hr markedly enhanced both GVBD (39.5 ± 4.2% to 66.2 ± 4.2%) and ovulation (24.8 ± 3.7% to 72.1 ± 5.7%) compared with the control follicles.
source: Of particular significance was the finding that treating late stage II follicles with CiVP for 24 hr markedly enhanced both GVBD (39.5 ± 4.2% to 66.2 ± 4.2%) and ovulation (24.8 ± 3.7% to 72.1 ± 5.7%) compared with the control follicles (Figure 3B,C, Video 3, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Enhancement of GVBD and ovulation was not observed in the presence of inactive linear CiVP.
source: Such enhancement was not observed in the presence of inactive linear CiVP in which the cysteine residues are protected with N-ethylmaleimide, demonstrating the specificity of CiVP (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C using inactive linear CiVP as a control.

claim: CiVP-treated oocytes were competent for fertilization and embryonic development.
source: Moreover, CiVP-treated oocytes were competent for fertilization and embryonic development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—source data 1), confirming that the oocytes were actually mature.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro fertilization assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CiVP plays important roles in Ciona oocyte maturation and ovulation.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that CiVP plays important roles in Ciona oocyte maturation and ovulation, which led us to further investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing CiVP enhances GVBD and ovulation, and CiVP-treated oocytes are competent for fertilization.

claim: In mammals, the extracellular signal-related kinase (ERK) and MAPK/ERK kinase (MEK) signaling pathways are activated by VP.
source: In mammals, the extracellular signal-related kinase (ERK) and MAPK/ERK kinase (MEK) signaling pathways are activated by VP (Kumari et al., 2017; Chiu et al., 2002), and ERK plays a role in oocyte maturation in vertebrates (Richani and Gilchrist, 2018; Das and Arur, 2017; Fan and Sun, 2004; Sha et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Kumari et al., 2017; Chiu et al., 2002).

claim: ERK plays a role in oocyte maturation in vertebrates.
source: In mammals, the extracellular signal-related kinase (ERK) and MAPK/ERK kinase (MEK) signaling pathways are activated by VP (Kumari et al., 2017; Chiu et al., 2002), and ERK plays a role in oocyte maturation in vertebrates (Richani and Gilchrist, 2018; Das and Arur, 2017; Fan and Sun, 2004; Sha et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Richani and Gilchrist, 2018; Das and Arur, 2017; Fan and Sun, 2004; Sha et al., 2017).

claim: The expression of CiErk1/2 was elevated throughout follicle development.
source: We found that the expression of CiErk1/2 (KH.L153.20) was elevated throughout follicle development (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1) and localized to oocytes and test cells during most stages, including the identical stage in CiVpr-expressing oocytes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: CiErk1/2 localized to oocytes and test cells during most stages.
source: We found that the expression of CiErk1/2 (KH.L153.20) was elevated throughout follicle development (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1) and localized to oocytes and test cells during most stages, including the identical stage in CiVpr-expressing oocytes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Inhibition of MEK/ERK activity in early stage III follicles using the MEK inhibitor U0126 resulted in significant decreases in the rates of both GVBD (86.2 ± 3.1% to 20.5 ± 9.0%) and ovulation (54.3 ± 5.8% to 6.4 ± 4.5%).
source: Inhibition of MEK/ERK activity in early stage III follicles using the MEK inhibitor U0126 resulted in significant decreases in the rates of both GVBD (86.2 ± 3.1% to 20.5 ± 9.0%) and ovulation (54.3 ± 5.8% to 6.4 ± 4.5%, Figure 3E,F, Video 4, and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: CiErk1/2 plays crucial roles in both oocyte maturation and ovulation.
source: Collectively, these results indicated that CiErk1/2 plays crucial roles in both oocyte maturation and ovulation and further suggest that CiVP signaling is mediated by CiErk1/2.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing MEK inhibition decreases GVBD and ovulation rates.

claim: CiVP signaling is mediated by CiErk1/2.
source: Collectively, these results indicated that CiErk1/2 plays crucial roles in both oocyte maturation and ovulation and further suggest that CiVP signaling is mediated by CiErk1/2.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results showing CiVP enhances GVBD/ovulation and MEK inhibition blocks these processes.

claim: Extensive phosphorylation of CiErk1/2 occurred at 5–10 min after CiVP stimulation.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of de-folliculated oocytes revealed extensive phosphorylation of CiErk1/2 at 5–10 min after CiVP stimulation, whereas no induction was observed in MEK-inhibited follicles (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No induction of CiErk1/2 phosphorylation was observed in MEK-inhibited follicles.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of de-folliculated oocytes revealed extensive phosphorylation of CiErk1/2 at 5–10 min after CiVP stimulation, whereas no induction was observed in MEK-inhibited follicles (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The RNA-seq data revealed no significant changes in the expression of CiCdk1 or CiCcnb in MEK-inhibited follicles.
source: The RNA-seq data revealed no significant changes in the expression of CiCdk1 or CiCcnb in MEK-inhibited follicles (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that MPF is regulated post-translationally in Ciona, as in other animals (Richani and Gilchrist, 2018; Nagahama and Yamashita, 2008; Kishimoto, 2018; Das and Arur, 2017; Fan and Sun, 2004).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: MPF is regulated post-translationally in Ciona.
source: The RNA-seq data revealed no significant changes in the expression of CiCdk1 or CiCcnb in MEK-inhibited follicles (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A and Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that MPF is regulated post-translationally in Ciona, as in other animals (Richani and Gilchrist, 2018; Nagahama and Yamashita, 2008; Kishimoto, 2018; Das and Arur, 2017; Fan and Sun, 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of transcriptional changes in MPF components and supported by citations to similar findings in other animals.

claim: The selective Cdc2 inhibitor Ro-3306 inhibited GVBD in late stage III follicles.
source: The selective Cdc2 inhibitor Ro-3306 inhibited GVBD in late stage III follicles (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1), confirming that MPF activity is also necessary for GVBD in Ciona.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MPF activity is necessary for GVBD in Ciona.
source: The selective Cdc2 inhibitor Ro-3306 inhibited GVBD in late stage III follicles (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1), confirming that MPF activity is also necessary for GVBD in Ciona.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental result showing Cdc2 inhibition blocks GVBD.

claim: CiVP-directed GVBD using late stage II follicles was completely blocked by MPF inhibition.
source: Notably, CiVP-directed GVBD using late stage II follicles was completely blocked by MPF inhibition (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1), indicating that MPF is required for the induction of GVBD by CiVP.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MPF is required for the induction of GVBD by CiVP.
source: Notably, CiVP-directed GVBD using late stage II follicles was completely blocked by MPF inhibition (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1), indicating that MPF is required for the induction of GVBD by CiVP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental result showing MPF inhibition blocks CiVP-induced GVBD.

claim: CiVP is a key molecule in the initiation of oocyte maturation via the MEK/ERK-MPF pathway in Ciona oocytes.
source: Consequently, these results led to the conclusion that CiVP is a key molecule in the initiation of oocyte maturation via the MEK/ERK-MPF pathway in Ciona oocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing CiVP activates ERK, ERK is required for GVBD, and MPF is required for CiVP-induced GVBD.

claim: In medaka, three MMPs (MMP-2, MMP-14, MMP-15) have been identified as essential enzymes for ovulation.
source: In medaka, a teleost fish species, three MMPs (MMP-2, MMP-14, MMP-15) have been identified as essential enzymes for ovulation (Ogiwara et al., 2005), but no proteases have been identified as essential for mammalian ovulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Ogiwara et al., 2005).

claim: No proteases have been identified as essential for mammalian ovulation.
source: In medaka, a teleost fish species, three MMPs (MMP-2, MMP-14, MMP-15) have been identified as essential enzymes for ovulation (Ogiwara et al., 2005), but no proteases have been identified as essential for mammalian ovulation.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The expression of only CiMmp2/9/13 declined by approximately 80% in MEK-inhibited follicles compared with the control.
source: Of these six genes, the expression of only CiMmp2/9/13 (KH.L76.4) declined by approximately 80% in MEK-inhibited follicles compared with the control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: qRT-PCR analysis using MEK-inhibited follicles revealed a significant 70% decrease in CiMmp2/9/13 mRNA levels.
source: The results of qRT-PCR analysis using MEK-inhibited follicles also revealed a significant 70% decrease in CiMmp2/9/13 mRNA levels (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CiVP stimulation of late stage II follicles resulted in a 4.0-fold upregulation of CiMmp2/9/13 expression.
source: Notably, CiVP stimulation of late stage II follicles resulted in a 4.0-fold upregulation of CiMmp2/9/13 expression (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1), confirming that CiVP induces CiMmp2/9/13 expression via MEK/ERK signaling during ovulation.
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CiVP induces CiMmp2/9/13 expression via MEK/ERK signaling during ovulation.
source: Notably, CiVP stimulation of late stage II follicles resulted in a 4.0-fold upregulation of CiMmp2/9/13 expression (Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1), confirming that CiVP induces CiMmp2/9/13 expression via MEK/ERK signaling during ovulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results showing CiVP upregulates CiMmp2/9/13 and MEK inhibition downregulates CiMmp2/9/13.

claim: CiMMP2/9/13 is localized in oocytes and outer follicular cells.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed that CiMMP2/9/13 protein localized in oocytes and the outer follicular cell layer of late stage III follicles (Figure 5C), and this result was in good agreement with the localization of CiVPR (Figure 3A) and CiErk1/2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of CiMMP2/9/13 resulted in a significant decrease in the ovulation rate (91.5 ± 3.2% to 41.4 ± 3.1%).
source: As expected, inhibition of CiMMP2/9/13 resulted in a significant decrease in the ovulation rate (91.5 ± 3.2% to 41.4 ± 3.1%), compared with uninhibited follicles (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5D using MMP-2/9 inhibitor II.

claim: CiVP-induced ovulation via upregulation of CiMMP2/9/13 in late stage II follicles was completely blocked by MMP-2/9 inhibitor II.
source: It is noteworthy that CiVP-induced ovulation via upregulation of CiMMP2/9/13 in late stage II follicles was completely blocked by MMP-2/9 inhibitor II (Figure 5E and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CiMMP2/9/13 expression is induced by CiVP via CiErk1/2 in oocytes and plays a pivotal role in Ciona ovulation.
source: Collectively, these results indicated that CiMMP2/9/13 expression is induced by CiVP via CiErk1/2 in oocytes and plays a pivotal role in Ciona ovulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing CiVP upregulates CiMMP2/9/13 via ERK and MMP inhibition blocks ovulation.

claim: Incubation of rCiMMP2/9/13 with DQ collagen type I or type IV in vitro resulted in significant digestion of these collagens.
source: Incubation of rCiMMP2/9/13 with putative substrates DQ collagen (fluorescent dye and its quencher are conjugated) type I or type IV in vitro resulted in significant digestion of these collagens, but collagen digestion was inhibited by MMP-2/9 inhibitor II.
evidence: This is based on in vitro collagenase activity assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Collagen digestion by rCiMMP2/9/13 was inhibited by MMP-2/9 inhibitor II.
source: Incubation of rCiMMP2/9/13 with putative substrates DQ collagen (fluorescent dye and its quencher are conjugated) type I or type IV in vitro resulted in significant digestion of these collagens, but collagen digestion was inhibited by MMP-2/9 inhibitor II.
evidence: This is based on in vitro collagenase activity assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Potent collagenase activity was observed in the outer follicular cell layer in the presence of DQ collagen type I or type IV.
source: While no activity was observed in oocytes, test cells, and follicular cells in ovulating follicles, potent collagenase activity was observed in the outer follicular cell layer in the presence of DQ collagen type I or type IV (Figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ zymography data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The outer follicular layer of post-ovulatory follicles exhibited high activity toward collagen type I and type IV.
source: Intriguingly, the outer follicular layer of post-ovulatory follicles also exhibited high activity toward collagen type I and type IV.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ zymography data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CiVP induces CiMMP2/9/13 expression via CiVPR-MEK/ERK signaling in oocytes and secreted CiMMP2/9/13 digests collagens type I and type IV in the outer follicular cell layer, causing the follicle to rupture with subsequent liberation of oocytes from the ovary.
source: Collectively, these results led to the conclusion that CiVP induces CiMMP2/9/13 expression via CiVPR-MEK/ERK signaling in oocytes and that secreted CiMMP2/9/13 digests collagens type I and type IV in the outer follicular cell layer, which causes the follicle to rupture, with subsequent liberation of oocytes from the ovary (i.e., ovulation).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental results showing the entire pathway from CiVP to ovulation.

claim: Oocyte maturation and ovulation are regulated by the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis (HPG axis) in vertebrates.
source: In vertebrates, oocyte maturation and ovulation are regulated by the hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal axis (HPG axis); gonadotropins from the pituitary stimulate the maturation of follicles in response to hypothalamic peptide hormones, including gonadotropin-releasing hormone (Richani and Gilchrist, 2018; Das and Arur, 2017; Nagahama and Yamashita, 2008; Fan and Sun, 2004; Kishimoto, 2018; Von Stetina and Orr-Weaver, 2011; Richards and Ascoli, 2018; Takahashi et al., 2018; Richards and Pangas, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Neither a pituitary organ nor gonadotropins arose in most species of invertebrates.
source: In contrast, neither a pituitary organ nor gonadotropins arose in most species of invertebrates, indicating the presence of HPG axis–independent regulation in these organisms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Some neuropeptides have been shown to induce oocyte maturation and ovulation (or spawning) in several species of invertebrates.
source: Some neuropeptides have been shown to induce oocyte maturation and ovulation (or spawning) in several species of invertebrates.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations to specific examples (Takeda et al., 2018; Mita et al., 2009; Kato et al., 2009).

claim: The neuropeptide W/RPRPamide in jellyfish directly induces oocyte maturation and spawning.
source: The neuropeptide W/RPRPamide in jellyfish directly induces oocyte maturation and spawning (Takeda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Takeda et al., 2018).

claim: A relaxin-like peptide stimulates the production of 1-methyladenosine, which directly induces oocyte maturation, followed by ovulation and spawning.
source: A relaxin-like peptide stimulates the production of 1-methyladenosine, which directly induces oocyte maturation, followed by ovulation and spawning (Mita et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Mita et al., 2009).

claim: Cubifurin (NGIWYamide) induces oocyte maturation, ovulation, and spawning in the sea cucumber.
source: Cubifurin (NGIWYamide) induces oocyte maturation, ovulation, and spawning in the sea cucumber (Kato et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Kato et al., 2009).

claim: Various neuropeptides are responsible for triggering oocyte maturation and ovulation in invertebrates.
source: These findings demonstrate that various neuropeptides are responsible for triggering oocyte maturation and ovulation in invertebrates, and suggest that oocyte maturation and ovulation and their underlying molecular mechanisms are regulated in both a species-specific and evolutionarily conserved fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples of different neuropeptides in different invertebrate species cited above.

claim: Oocyte maturation and ovulation and their underlying molecular mechanisms are regulated in both a species-specific and evolutionarily conserved fashion.
source: These findings demonstrate that various neuropeptides are responsible for triggering oocyte maturation and ovulation in invertebrates, and suggest that oocyte maturation and ovulation and their underlying molecular mechanisms are regulated in both a species-specific and evolutionarily conserved fashion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of both diversity (different neuropeptides) and commonality (neuropeptidergic regulation) across species.

claim: Ascidians are invertebrates that belong to the Chordata superphylum as Urochordata.
source: Ascidians are invertebrates that belong to the Chordata superphylum as Urochordata, and thus, phylogenetically, they are the closest living relatives of vertebrates (Delsuc et al., 2006; Denoeud et al., 2010; Satoh et al., 2014; Horie et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Ascidians are considered crucial model organisms in research into the evolutionary processes underlying chordate reproductive systems.
source: As such, ascidians are considered crucial model organisms in research into the evolutionary processes underlying chordate reproductive systems.
evidence: This is inferred from their phylogenetic position as the closest living relatives of vertebrates.

claim: A variety of vertebrate prototypic neuropeptides were identified from the neural complex of Ciona intestinalis Type A.
source: Our previous studies identified a variety of vertebrate prototypic neuropeptides from the neural complex of the cosmopolitan ascidian, Ciona intestinalis Type A (Ciona robusta) (Kawada et al., 2011; Brunetti et al., 2015), and we revealed the full trajectory of visceral nerves to the ovary (Osugi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors (Kawada et al., 2011; Brunetti et al., 2015).

claim: The full trajectory of visceral nerves to the ovary was revealed in Ciona.
source: Our previous studies identified a variety of vertebrate prototypic neuropeptides from the neural complex of the cosmopolitan ascidian, Ciona intestinalis Type A (Ciona robusta) (Kawada et al., 2011; Brunetti et al., 2015), and we revealed the full trajectory of visceral nerves to the ovary (Osugi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors (Osugi et al., 2017).

claim: Several cognate receptors were shown to be expressed in the ovary.
source: Moreover, several cognate receptors were shown to be expressed in the ovary (Kawada et al., 2008; Satake et al., 2004; Sekiguchi et al., 2012; Tello et al., 2005; Shiraishi et al., 2019), and some neuropeptides, such as Ciona tachykinin and neurotensin-like peptide 6, were found to participate in regulating pre-GVBD follicle growth (Aoyama et al., 2008; Aoyama et al., 2012; Kawada et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Kawada et al., 2008; Satake et al., 2004; Sekiguchi et al., 2012; Tello et al., 2005; Shiraishi et al., 2019).

claim: Some neuropeptides, such as Ciona tachykinin and neurotensin-like peptide 6, were found to participate in regulating pre-GVBD follicle growth.
source: Moreover, several cognate receptors were shown to be expressed in the ovary (Kawada et al., 2008; Satake et al., 2004; Sekiguchi et al., 2012; Tello et al., 2005; Shiraishi et al., 2019), and some neuropeptides, such as Ciona tachykinin and neurotensin-like peptide 6, were found to participate in regulating pre-GVBD follicle growth (Aoyama et al., 2008; Aoyama et al., 2012; Kawada et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Aoyama et al., 2008; Aoyama et al., 2012; Kawada et al., 2011).

claim: Neuropeptides play vital roles in oocyte maturation and ovulation in Ciona.
source: These findings, considered in the context of the lack of a pituitary organ and gonadotropins, strongly suggest that neuropeptides also play vital roles in oocyte maturation and ovulation in Ciona.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of neuropeptides and their receptors in the ovary, combined with the absence of the HPG axis.

claim: Ciona meiosis is arrested at ProI, resumes under stimulation by an as yet unidentified factor, and is arrested again at MetI after oocyte maturation and ovulation.
source: Ciona meiosis is arrested at ProI, resumes under stimulation by an as yet unidentified factor, and is arrested again at MetI after oocyte maturation and ovulation (Tosti et al., 2011; Von Stetina and Orr-Weaver, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Tosti et al., 2011; Von Stetina and Orr-Weaver, 2011).

claim: The importance of pH and levels of cAMP and/or Ca2+ in Ciona GVBD in artificial seawater (ASW) was previously demonstrated.
source: The importance of pH and levels of cAMP and/or Ca2+ in Ciona GVBD in artificial seawater (ASW) was previously demonstrated (Silvestre et al., 2009; Silvestre et al., 2011; Tosti et al., 2011; Lambert, 2008; Lambert, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Silvestre et al., 2009; Silvestre et al., 2011; Tosti et al., 2011; Lambert, 2008; Lambert, 2011).

claim: The activities of MAP kinase (MAPK) and maturation promoting factor (MPF) function after fertilization in Ciona.

claim: Common chordate ancestors might have adopted the MEK/ERK-MMP pathway, which is also conserved in Ciona ovulation.
source: Considered along with the aforementioned involvement of MMPs in ovulation in vertebrates, the present data regarding the MEK/ERK-MMP regulatory pathway in Ciona ovulation suggest the following three-step evolutionary process: i) common chordate ancestors might have adopted the MEK/ERK-MMP pathway, which is also conserved in Ciona ovulation; ii) MEK/ERK regulation in fish might have been lost or compensated by other regulators, given that an MEK/ERK-directed ovulatory mechanism has been demonstrated in mammals; and iii) the roles of various proteases, including MMPs, in vertebrate ovulatory regulation have diversified during the evolutionary process (Figure 7—figure supplement 1i-iii).
evidence: This is speculated based on the comparative analysis of ovulatory mechanisms in Ciona, fish, and mammals.

claim: VP/OT family peptide–directed regulation of oocyte maturation and ovulation might have originated in ancestral chordates.
